nameStory: The Ashtray Bolete gets its rather unappetizing name from its distinctive odor, which many foragers describe as reminiscent of stale cigarette smoke or old ashtrays. When you cut into the flesh or handle older specimens, this acrid, smoky smell becomes quite noticeable and is actually one of the best ways to identify this mushroom in the field.
description: The Ashtray Bolete is a medium-sized mushroom with the characteristic spongy pore surface underneath its cap instead of gills, marking it as a member of the bolete family. It typically grows 3-6 inches tall with caps ranging from 2-5 inches across. The mushroom has a brownish to reddish-brown cap and often shows small red dots or patches on its pale stem, giving it the 'rubropunctum' part of its scientific name (meaning 'red-dotted'). Like many boletes, it has a sturdy, club-shaped stem and thick, meaty flesh.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Cut flesh or bruised areas emit a distinctive acrid, smoky odor reminiscent of stale tobacco or old ashtrays - this is the most reliable identifying feature

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Brown to reddish-brown surface that feels slightly velvety when young, becoming smoother with age; may crack in dry weather revealing paler flesh beneath

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Tiny yellow pores underneath the cap that may bruise blue when pressed; pores are small enough that the surface looks almost smooth from a distance

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Pale yellow to whitish stem often decorated with small red dots or reddish patches, especially near the top; feels firm and solid when squeezed

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Flesh may slowly turn blue when cut or damaged, though this reaction is often faint and inconsistent compared to other blue-staining boletes

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Produces an olive-brown spore print when cap is placed gill-side down on white paper overnight

habitat: Look for Ashtray Boletes in mixed hardwood and coniferous forests throughout New England, particularly under oak, beech, and pine trees. They form beneficial partnerships (mycorrhizal relationships) with tree roots and prefer well-drained, slightly acidic soils. You'll often find them on slopes or raised areas rather than in wet, boggy spots.

seasonality.spring: Rarely fruits in spring, though very early specimens might appear in late May during warm, wet years following the first humid spells.
seasonality.summer: Prime fruiting season begins in mid to late summer, especially after periods of rain followed by warm, humid weather that's perfect for mushroom development.
seasonality.fall: Peak season continues through early fall, with the best specimens often found in September and early October before the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: No fresh fruiting occurs, though you might find dried, blackened remnants clinging to the forest floor as evidence of the previous season's growth.

funFact: Despite its off-putting smoky smell, some European foragers actually prize the Ashtray Bolete for cooking because the unpleasant odor completely disappears when heated, leaving behind a pleasant, nutty flavor - though you should never attempt to eat any wild mushroom without expert identification first!
confusionNotes: The Ashtray Bolete is most easily confused with other brown-capped boletes, but the distinctive smoky smell when cut is usually enough to separate it from look-alikes. Remember the phrase 'smoky smell, red dots tell' - the combination of the acrid odor and reddish stem markings are your best identification clues.
contextualKnowledge: **Note: I have limited training data on this specific species, so some details may be uncertain.** The genus Hemileccinum was only recently separated from other bolete genera through DNA analysis, so older field guides may list this species under different scientific names. This is part of ongoing efforts to better understand bolete relationships and classification.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives in the Hemileccinum genus, the Ashtray Bolete is distinguished primarily by its smoky odor and the red dotting on its stem. The Smoothish-stemmed Bolete lacks the distinctive smell and has a cleaner, less decorated stem surface, while the Corrugated Bolete typically shows more pronounced ridging or wrinkling on its cap surface. **Safety note: Never eat any wild mushroom without expert confirmation, as misidentification can be dangerous.**

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives in the Hemileccinum genus, the smoothish-stemmed bolete is the most commonly encountered in New England.
